chief_complaint: progressive breathlessness on climbing stairs, extreme fatigue, and chest tightness over 8 months
hpi_details: 8-month history of insidious, progressive shortness of breath when climbing stairs or walking uphill, which has now worsened to breathlessness when walking on flat ground. Accompanied by chronic severe fatigue, atypical dull chest tightness, and lightheadedness when exerting herself. Two weeks ago, she experienced a near-fainting episode (pre-syncope) while hurrying to catch a bus. Over the past month, noticed her ankles swelling in the evenings and fingers turning blue/white in cold air (Raynaud's phenomenon). Denies chronic cough, wheezing, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, or prior blood clots. Seen by three previous physicians who diagnosed anxiety and physical deconditioning.
ideas: thinks her heart is struggling to pump blood through narrowed lung blood vessels
concerns: terrified she has a fatal, progressive heart-lung condition after fainting on the street
expectations: wants right heart catheterization testing and specialized pulmonary vasodilator drugs to open her lung arteries
pmh: Raynaud's phenomenon for 5 years, mild gastro-oesophageal reflux, no history of deep vein thrombosis
social_hx: never smoked, zero alcohol, financial analyst, single

clinical_knowledge.topic: Pulmonary arterial hypertension evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of pulmonary arterial hypertension is essential for targeted diagnostic workup and referral to a specialist centre.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Exertional presyncope, right-heart-failure features, and exertional hypoxaemia require urgent clinical assessment and expedited referral to a pulmonary-hypertension centre.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive breathlessness on climbing stairs, extreme fatigue, and chest tightness over 8 months

Key HPI features: 8-month history of insidious, progressive shortness of breath when climbing stairs or walking uphill, which has now worsened to breathlessness when walking on flat ground. Accompanied by chronic severe fatigue, atypical dull chest tightness, and lightheadedness when exerting herself. Two weeks ago, she experienced a near-fainting episode (pre-syncope) while hurrying to catch a bus. Over the past month, noticed her ankles swelling in the evenings and fingers turning blue/white in cold air (Raynaud's phenomenon). Denies chronic cough, wheezing, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, or prior blood clots. Seen by three previous physicians who diagnosed anxiety and physical deconditioning.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: normal resting HR, O2 sat 94% on room air at rest dropping to 86% during 6-minute walk test. Cardiovascular exam: inspect JVP -> elevated with prominent a-waves. Palpation: prominent right ventricular heave/parasternal lift and palpable P2. Auscultation: loud, accentuated pulmonary component of second heart sound (loud P2), right-sided S3 gallop, and pansystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation at lower left sternal border increasing with inspiration (Carvallo's sign). Lung fields completely clear on auscultation. 12-lead ECG: right axis deviation, right ventricular hypertrophy with strain pattern (tall R in V1, deep S in V5/V6, right precordial T-wave inversions), and P-pulmonale. Transthoracic Echocardiogram (TTE): right ventricular dilation and hypertrophy, D-shaped left ventricle from interventricular septal flattening, and elevated estimated Pulmonary Artery Systolic Pressure (PASP >50 mmHg based on tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity). Gold-Standard Diagnostic Invasive Testing: Right Heart Catheterization (RHC) -> confirms resting Mean Pulmonary Arterial Pressure (mPAP) >= 20 mmHg, Pulmonary Vascular Resistance (PVR) > 2 Wood units, and normal Pulmonary Artery Wedge Pressure (PAWP <= 15 mmHg confirming Pre-Capillary Pulmonary Hypertension). Autoimmune screen: check anti-centromere / anti-Scl-70 antibodies to screen for Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma)-associated PAH.
Relevant background/PMH: Raynaud's phenomenon for 5 years, mild gastro-oesophageal reflux, no history of deep vein thrombosis
common_misconceptions: Attributing progressive exertional breathlessness and presyncope to anxiety or deconditioning without considering pulmonary hypertension.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Assuming pulmonary arterial hypertension without excluding left-heart disease, chronic lung disease, and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as exertional syncope or right-heart failure.
management_principles: Arrange urgent assessment and expedited referral to a pulmonary-hypertension centre; emergency evaluation is needed for syncope, worsening hypoxaemia, or decompensated right-heart failure.

An expert centre should confirm the haemodynamic diagnosis with right-heart catheterization and complete testing for pulmonary-hypertension group and cause, including V/Q scanning for chronic thromboembolic disease.
The specialist team may perform vasoreactivity testing only when indicated and select PAH-specific therapy after classification, risk assessment, contraindication review, and pregnancy counselling.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: European Society of Cardiology: Pulmonary Hypertension Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 34F with Raynaud's presents with 8-month progressive exertional dyspnoea, exertional presyncope, atypical chest tightness, and peripheral oedema. Misdiagnosed as anxiety.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: normal resting HR, O2 sat 94% on room air at rest dropping to 86% during 6-minute walk test. Cardiovascular exam: inspect JVP -> elevated with prominent a-waves. Palpation: prominent right ventricular heave/parasternal lift and palpable P2. Auscultation: loud, accentuated pulmonary component of second heart sound (loud P2), right-sided S3 gallop, and pansystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation at lower left sternal border increasing with inspiration (Carvallo's sign). Lung fields completely clear on auscultation. 12-lead ECG: right axis deviation, right ventricular hypertrophy with strain pattern (tall R in V1, deep S in V5/V6, right precordial T-wave inversions), and P-pulmonale. Transthoracic Echocardiogram (TTE): right ventricular dilation and hypertrophy, D-shaped left ventricle from interventricular septal flattening, and elevated estimated Pulmonary Artery Systolic Pressure (PASP >50 mmHg based on tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity). Gold-Standard Diagnostic Invasive Testing: Right Heart Catheterization (RHC) -> confirms resting Mean Pulmonary Arterial Pressure (mPAP) >= 20 mmHg, Pulmonary Vascular Resistance (PVR) > 2 Wood units, and normal Pulmonary Artery Wedge Pressure (PAWP <= 15 mmHg confirming Pre-Capillary Pulmonary Hypertension). Autoimmune screen: check anti-centromere / anti-Scl-70 antibodies to screen for Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma)-associated PAH.
reference_soap.assessment: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH - WHO Group 1 Pre-Capillary Pulmonary Hypertension, likely Idiopathic or Systemic Sclerosis-associated). DDx: Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH - WHO Group 4 -> must perform V/Q lung scan to rule out chronic mismatched perfusion defects), Left heart disease / diastolic heart failure (WHO Group 2 -> PAWP >15 mmHg), Chronic lung disease / COPD / ILD (WHO Group 3 -> abnormal spirometry/HRCT).
reference_soap.plan: Arrange urgent assessment and expedited referral to a pulmonary-hypertension centre because of exertional presyncope, oedema, and desaturation; seek emergency care for syncope, worsening breathlessness, persistent low oxygen levels, or signs of decompensated right-heart failure. The specialist centre should confirm and classify pulmonary hypertension with right-heart catheterization and V/Q scanning. PAH-specific medication, diuretics, anticoagulation, oxygen, and pregnancy counselling must be individualized and directed by the treating specialist.

learning_objectives: Identify classical physical signs of right ventricular strain: parasternal heave, loud P2, and Carvallo's sign of tricuspid regurgitation
Interpret Right Heart Catheterization hemodynamics confirming pre-capillary PAH (mPAP >=20 mmHg, PVR >2 Wood units, PAWP <=15 mmHg)
Differentiate WHO Group 1 PAH from Group 4 CTEPH utilizing mandatory Ventilation/Perfusion (V/Q) lung scanning
Formulate specialized pulmonary vasodilator combination regimens (endothelin antagonists plus PDE5 inhibitors) in expert centers

teaching.one_liner: A pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension syndrome causing progressive exertional dyspnoea, presyncope, and eventual right-heart failure.

must_ask.say: How far can you walk or climb before breathlessness makes you stop?
Have you felt faint or actually passed out during physical activity?
Have you developed ankle swelling, abdominal bloating, or rapid weight gain?
Do your fingers change colour in the cold, or have you had skin tightening, joint symptoms, or reflux?
Have you ever had a blood clot, or a family history of clots?

history.answer: I've been getting more and more short of breath whenever I climb stairs or walk uphill, and lately I even struggle when walking on flat ground.
It started very gradually about eight months ago and has been steadily getting worse ever since.
At first, I only noticed it after climbing a flight of stairs or walking up a hill, but now I get breathless just walking across a level parking lot.
It's constantly there whenever I exert myself; it doesn't come and go in sudden attacks.
No, I can lie completely flat with one pillow and I never wake up choking or gasping for air.
Any physical exertion brings it on, and cold weather also makes my fingers change color and feel numb.
No, I've never heard any whistling or wheezing sounds when I breathe.
No, I don't have a cough, I'm not bringing up any phlegm, and I haven't had any fevers or chills.
Yes, I get an uncomfortable dull tightness across my chest whenever I exert myself, though it's not a sharp stabbing pain.
I get very lightheaded when I push myself, and two weeks ago I nearly blacked out while hurrying to catch a bus.
My heart pounds fast when I get winded, but I haven't noticed any sudden fluttering or racing rhythms out of nowhere.
No, I have never coughed up any blood.
Over the past month, I've noticed both of my ankles getting puffy and swollen by the evening.
No, both legs look the same and I don't have any pain or calf cramps in either leg.
No, I haven't had any recent surgeries, I haven't been on any long flights, and I've never had a blood clot.
Yes, for about five years my fingers have turned white, then blue and painful whenever I'm in the cold or touch cold water.
I have mild acid reflux, but I don't have joint swelling, dry mouth, or tight thickened skin on my hands or face.
I feel overwhelmingly exhausted all the time, but I haven't noticed pale skin, dark stools, or unusually heavy periods.
I do feel anxious because I can't breathe, but I don't have tingling around my mouth or fingers, and it only happens when I'm physically active.
Three doctors told me it was just stress, anxiety, and being out of shape, but I've never had asthma, COPD, or heart disease.
I work in an office as a financial analyst, so I haven't been exposed to industrial dust, asbestos, birds, or mold.
No, I have never taken blood pressure pills, anti-inflammatory pain relievers, heart rhythm drugs, or chemotherapy.
I've had Raynaud's phenomenon for five years and mild acid reflux, but no other chronic illnesses.
I've never had any surgeries and I've never been admitted to a hospital.
I take omeprazole 20 milligrams once a day for my reflux, and nothing else.
I don't have any allergies to medications that I know of.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any nicotine products.
I don't drink any alcohol at all.
I'm single, I live by myself in an apartment, and I work full-time as a financial analyst.
No one in my family has had lung disease or serious heart problems at a young age.
My periods are regular every twenty-eight days, my last one was two weeks ago, and there is no chance I could be pregnant.
I've been reading and wondering if my heart is having trouble pumping blood through narrowed vessels in my lungs.
I'm terrified that this might be a progressive, fatal condition involving my heart and lungs, especially after almost passing out.

exam.finding: Alert, fatigued young woman breathing comfortably at rest without visible cyanosis or use of accessory muscles.
Blood pressure 116/76 mmHg, pulse 78 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, temperature 36.8°C.
Conjunctivae are pink with no pallor; sclerae are clear and non-icteric.
Elevated jugular venous pressure measured at 4 cm above the sternal angle with prominent a-waves.
Prominent right ventricular heave along the lower left sternal border and a palpable pulmonary closure sound.
Resonant to percussion across all lung fields bilaterally.
Normal vesicular breath sounds bilaterally; lung fields are completely clear with no wheezes or crackles.
Accentuated pulmonic component of S2, right-sided S3 gallop, and a holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border that increases with inspiration.
Bilateral mild pitting edema (1+) over both ankles and lower shins.
Calves are symmetric without tenderness, warmth, swelling, or palpable cords.
Fingers are cool with mild dusky blanching consistent with Raynaud phenomenon; no sclerodactyly, digital ulcers, or rash.
